claims.text: In single-phase, equiatomic HEAs, solid-solution strengthening is the primary mechanism governing hardness and strength.
Severe lattice distortion drives solid-solution strengthening in single-phase, equiatomic HEAs.
Greater atomic-size mismatch among constituent elements produces larger local strain fields.
Local strain fields caused by atomic-size mismatch hinder dislocation motion.
Hindered dislocation motion increases hardness and yield strength.
Replacing one constituent with an element of a distinctly different atomic radius will systematically alter atomic-size mismatch while single-phase stability is maintained.
Cold rolling followed by annealing at 600°C for 1 hour can be used to control grain size and residual stresses in the compared HEAs.
Lattice distortion raises the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
Relevant lattice distortions can be characterized using high-resolution TEM.
The impedance to dislocation movement is stronger in alloys having larger atomic-size mismatches.
HEAs with enhanced atomic-size mismatch and greater lattice distortion will have higher hardness than a similarly processed low-mismatch baseline HEA.
HEAs with enhanced atomic-size mismatch and greater lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than a similarly processed low-mismatch baseline HEA.
A composition selected to minimize atomic-size differences will exhibit less pronounced lattice distortion.
The proposed governing behavior is limited to single-phase HEAs without secondary precipitates or ordering phenomena.
The proposed governing behavior applies at room temperature when dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates.
At elevated temperatures, diffusion-related mechanisms may become significant.
In multiphase alloys, precipitation strengthening or other mechanisms may become significant.
Electronic factors and short-range order may contribute to the measured strengthening.
Grain size may modify the magnitude of strengthening attributed to atomic-size mismatch.
Failure of the higher-mismatch alloys to show a statistically significant increase in both hardness and yield strength relative to the control would falsify the proposed dominant mechanism.
